title: The Spear and the Water Jug
summary: The Ziphites betray David's hiding place again, and Saul comes after him with three thousand men. David and Abishai slip into Saul's sleeping camp, and David refuses to let Abishai kill the LORD's anointed, taking only Saul's spear and water jug. From a distant hilltop he shames Abner for failing to guard the king and pleads with Saul, who confesses his wrong and blesses David before they part for the last time.
story: This is the second time David has Saul in his power and lets him go. In chapter 24 the opportunity fell into his lap in a cave; here David goes looking for it, walking into the middle of Saul's army at night. The episode comes right after the Nabal story, where David learned that the LORD deals with those who wrong him, and David now states that lesson in his own words: the LORD will strike Saul down in his own time. This is the last meeting between Saul and David. Saul will be dead within a few chapters, and David will never see him again. The chapter's final exchange, a blessing from Saul and a parting of ways, ends their long, tragic relationship with a word of truth from the king who had tried so often to kill him.
historical:
The setting is again the Wilderness of Ziph, the rugged country southeast of Hebron toward the Dead Sea, where the people of the town of Ziph had already once reported David to Saul (1 Samuel 23:19). Jeshimon means wasteland and refers to the barren slopes of the Judean wilderness. Saul's three thousand chosen men are a standing force, which Saul had begun to gather early in his reign (13:2), and the commander Abner son of Ner was Saul's cousin (14:50).

Two of David's men are named. Ahimelech the Hittite shows that David's band included foreigners; the Hittites of the Bible were people of Hittite descent living in Canaan, and a later Hittite in David's service, Uriah, will play a tragic part in 2 Samuel 11. Abishai son of Zeruiah is David's nephew (Zeruiah was David's sister, 1 Chronicles 2:16), and with his brothers Joab and Asahel he will be a fierce, often ruthless presence throughout David's reign.
cultural:
Saul's spear, stuck upright in the ground by his head, marks where the king sleeps; it is almost his scepter. It is also the weapon Saul had thrown at David (18:11, 19:10) and at his own son Jonathan (20:33). David's taking it is a silent statement that he could have used it and did not. The water jug was essential in the desert, and taking it proves how close David had come.

David's plea in verse 19 reflects an ancient conviction that the LORD was worshiped in his own land and among his own people. To be driven out of Israel's inheritance was to be pushed toward the gods of other lands, as if the exile were saying, go, serve other gods. David is not saying the LORD is limited to one country but that being hunted out of the community of God's people cuts him off from the worship of God among them. His image of the king chasing a flea, or hunting a partridge (a bird pursued on foot until it tires), mocks the absurdity of Israel's king spending his army on one fugitive.
literary: The chapter deliberately parallels chapter 24: Saul pursues with three thousand men, David is urged by a companion to kill him, David refuses because Saul is the LORD's anointed, takes a token as proof, calls out to Saul from a distance, and Saul confesses and calls David my son. The differences sharpen the lesson. Here David takes the initiative, the token is a weapon rather than a scrap of robe, and David does not even have to fight his own conscience. The deep sleep from the LORD (verse 12) shows that God himself delivered Saul into David's hand, which makes the refusal to strike all the more deliberate. A touch of irony runs through David's taunt of Abner: he rebukes the general for failing to guard the anointed king, which is exactly what David himself has been doing. Saul's confession, “I have played the fool”, recalls Samuel's first rebuke of Saul for acting foolishly (13:13).

outline.t: The Ziphites inform, and Saul pursues
David spares Saul in the sleeping camp
Saul's confession and blessing; they part

doctrines.note: David leaves Saul's fate to the LORD: “the LORD Himself will strike him down; either his day will come and he will die, or he will go into battle and perish.” He trusts that God can remove Saul without David's help, and the deep sleep from the LORD shows God's hand over the whole scene.

The word anointed (mashiach) appears four times. David will not raise his hand against the LORD's anointed because the office belongs to God, not to the one who holds it. This reverence for the anointed king is the soil in which the later hope for the Messiah, the Anointed One, grows.

Saul says, “I have sinned,” and admits he has played the fool. His words are true, but there is no lasting change; he goes home and David still has to flee. The chapter shows that confession can be sincere in the moment and still fall short of the turning that repentance means.

words.note: Mashiach, anointed, from the verb to smear or pour oil. Kings, priests, and occasionally prophets were anointed as a sign that God had set them apart. The Greek translation of the word is christos, from which the title Christ comes. David's four uses of it here show that his restraint is theological: to strike Saul would be to strike at the LORD's own appointment.

Tardemah, deep sleep. It is used for the sleep God brings on Adam before forming Eve (Genesis 2:21) and on Abram at the covenant ceremony (Genesis 15:12). Here it signals that the sleep of Saul's whole camp is not luck but the LORD's doing, which makes the moment a real test: God has put Saul in David's hand, and David still will not strike.

Nachalah, inheritance, the land allotted to each tribe and family as its share in God's gift. Being driven from the inheritance of the LORD meant being cut off from the land and people where the LORD was worshiped. David's lament shows that his exile is not only physical danger but spiritual loss.

Tsedaqah, righteousness, paired in verse 23 with faithfulness. David asks the LORD to repay each person according to these. Righteousness in the Old Testament is conduct that is right within a relationship; David's sparing of Saul is righteousness because he keeps faith with his king even while his king breaks faith with him.

christ: David's refusal to seize the throne by force, even when God seems to put it within reach, anticipates a pattern completed in Jesus. The anointed son of David did not grasp power but received the kingdom from the Father by the road of the cross (Philippians 2:6-11 describes Christ as not treating equality with God as something to be exploited). When his follower drew a sword to defend him in the garden, Jesus told him to put it away, much as David restrains Abishai. The connection is a pattern of character rather than a prediction. The word anointed itself also ties the chapter to the whole story: the reverence David shows the LORD's anointed prepares for the one the New Testament calls the Christ.
questions: Abishai tells David that God has delivered his enemy into his hand. How can a person tell the difference between an opportunity God gives and a temptation that looks like one?
Saul's confession is sincere but produces no lasting change. What distinguishes feeling sorry from truly turning around?
David grieves being driven from the worshiping community as much as from safety. How much do you value belonging to God's people, and what would you miss if you lost it?
